source.title: Connecting the geometry and dynamics of many-body complex systems with message passing neural operators
source.authors: Nicholas Gabriel; Neil F. Johnson; G. Karniadakis

record.tranche_reason: The study extends parameter-count scaling experiments to scientific neural operators for two many-body dynamics systems; it does not test language-model pretraining scaling.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own parameter-count sweeps and power-law fits for forecast and PDE losses. Comparisons to Kaplan et al. and the CViT exponents from Bahri et al. are cited results, not new experiments by this study, so they are not recorded as rows. It does not test language-model held-out loss, compute-optimal allocation, downstream task predictability, or fixed-parameter architecture shape.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own ROMA neural operators at three parameter counts on two graph-dynamics systems and fits L(P)=(Pc/P)^αP to forecast and PDE losses (Tables 5–6). That is a test of whether the power-law form holds outside text pretraining (V5), in a non-language scientific setting. The CViT exponents in Table 6 are cited from another paper and are not this study's results.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also state that PDE-loss exponents are an order of magnitude larger than forecast exponents. They also state that, with high topological heterogeneity, architecture matters more than size. They suggest power-law scaling might differentiate systems by degree of hierarchality. The scaling-regime differences are attributed to topological heterogeneity and dynamical effects.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales scientific neural operators by parameter count and measures forecast and PDE losses on graph-based dynamics, rather than measuring language-model held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported exponents differ by dataset and loss measure; the authors relate this to topological heterogeneity and dynamical effects.

fits_no_version.finding: For ROMA (DeepONet-style), the authors report that performance gains came mostly from transformer embedding dim and basis dim p, with little benefit beyond 7 layers and 8 heads. They contrast this with shape-insensitive standard transformers. The finding is stated in text only and is not at fixed parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In product-structured neural operators, the scaling benefit depends on which width dimension is scaled, unlike standard transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors conclude that under high topological heterogeneity, architecture matters more than model size. This rests on the equal-parameter architecture comparisons in Tables 2–3 plus weak size scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In topologically heterogeneous systems, architectural choice dominates parameter scaling.

record.problems: The parameter-count scaling results cover three model sizes per system. No uncertainty estimates for the reported fits are stated. The PDE loss for BD-3M is not monotonic across all three sizes.
record.rows_left_out: No own scaling results omitted. The cited CViT and language-model scaling figures are excluded because they are results from other work.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss; scaling in tokens or compute; ranges of several orders of magnitude.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger ones.
Effect of shape at fixed parameter count.
Scaling in data or compute. Parameter ranges wider than about 4–5x. Image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer.
Downstream task predictability from scale or loss.
Fitting method, parameter-counting convention and schedule choices. Curvature away from a single power law, which cannot be assessed with 3 points.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling evidence is thin: 3 sizes per system, spanning about 4–5x in parameters, with no uncertainty and no fit diagnostics. Training iterations vary (50k–100k, depending on experiment), which may confound the size comparison. The comparison to LLM exponents (Kaplan) and the CViT fits are cited, not new results. The KM-3M ROMA-B forecast value in Table 5 (1.29e-3) differs from the 264M ROMA value in Tables 2–3 (1.46e-3). The setups probably differ (e.g., positional embedding), but the study does not explain this.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Comparisons of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests scaling in scientific dynamical-system operators, not image/video modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
It does not test language-model setup choices, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, fitting methods, compute-optimal splits, or bends away from a power law.

relationships.condition: ROMA forecast loss (KM-3M, BD-3M) and PDE loss (KM-3M) vs parameter count
relationships.reason: Losses fall monotonically with parameters and the authors fit power laws (r13, r14, r15). The evidence rests on only 3 points over under one decade.
relationships.display_finding: Losses decreased monotonically with parameters and fitted power laws across three measurements spanning less than one decade.

relationships.reason: PDE loss rises from ROMA-L to ROMA-H (r11, r12). The reported power law (r16) is fitted to non-monotonic data.
relationships.display_finding: PDE loss increased from ROMA-L to ROMA-H, making the data underlying the reported power-law fit non-monotonic.

relationships.condition: Across the two graph systems and the two loss measures
relationships.reason: Fitted αP ranges from 0.022 to 1.459 depending on system and loss (r13–r16), so exponents depend on data/setup. These are dataset differences, not fitting-method choices.
relationships.display_finding: The fitted exponent αP ranges from 0.022 to 1.459 across systems and loss measures, reflecting dataset and measurement differences.
